title: How I Taught "The Novel" at the College Level
author: Matt Spivey
summary: A former college literature instructor lays out, book by book, how he structured his The Novel survey course -- eight full novels per semester, three scaffolded essays, two student-led discussion days, and an in-class final. His central argument is pedagogical stubbornness: against the common complaint that students today can't or won't read that much, he insists the fix is simply holding a firm standard and enforcing accountability. He walks through his actual course sequence and the reasoning behind each pairing -- Frankenstein for morality and psychology, Moby Dick as a monthlong centerpiece, Portrait of the Artist or Gatsby for modernism, Black No More or Passing for race and the Harlem Renaissance, and Maus or Player Piano to close on postmodernism -- showing how alternating options let him vary emphasis year to year without abandoning the course's spine. He's candid that his list leaves out major names (Austen, Eliot, Dostoyevsky, Morrison) and frames that omission as an unavoidable tradeoff of any single-semester survey rather than a flaw to apologize for.
points: The author built his college Novel survey course around eight full novels per semester plus three scaffolded essays and two student-led discussions, arguing accountability -- not shorter reading loads -- is the answer to declining student reading stamina.

His selection method was deliberately mixed (chronological, thematic, author-based, and personal preference) rather than a fixed canon, using pairs to let the same course slot serve different thematic emphases year to year.
He frames choosing course texts as inherently a tradeoff exercise, naming major omissions upfront rather than pretending any single-semester survey can be comprehensive.
The piece doubles as a template: he details his three graded assignments and offers to share them with any teacher who asks.
quotes: I always taught eight novels in a semester. I know, you're thinking, "How do I get students to read that many books in just one semester?" You make them -- that's all there is to it. Accountability is everything.

Hardly a week goes by anymore where we don't hear about the "end of reading" and professors complaining that their students can't/won't complete class texts. But I refuse to accept the idea that kids today just can't/won't read that many pages.

Moby Dick -- I think it's the best novel ever written, and though it is very intimidating (it usually took us a full month to complete), students would really get into the adventure of it and the relationships of the shipmen.

Black No More OR Passing -- These are great texts for incorporating discussions of race and identity and the Harlem Renaissance as a cultural influence. One is satirical, one is tragic, and both deal with the sometimes-confusing distinctions between black and white.
With eight books, three papers, two discussion tasks, and an in-class short essay final exam, this was a busy class. But, hey, that is what college-level work should entail.
Yes, Austen and Eliot and Dostoyevsky and Steinbeck and Morrison and Hemingway and others are missing.
